conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for coming in today. My name is Dr. Lee, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I specialize in helping new mothers navigate the emotional ups and downs that can come after childbirth.  

I’d like to spend a few minutes with the EPDS—that’s the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. It’s a short, well-studied questionnaire that helps us see how you’ve been feeling emotionally over the past week. It isn’t a test of your parenting; it’s simply a way for us to pick up on any signs of depression, anxiety, or distress so we can make sure you get the support you deserve.  

Everything we discuss stays confidential. My goal is to create a safe, non-judgmental space where you can answer honestly. There are just ten questions; I’ll ask each one conversationally, and you can answer in your own words—no need to worry about choosing from a list.  

If at any point you feel uncomfortable, we can pause. Ready to begin?  

Here’s the first question:  
Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

[slow half-shrug, eyes on the floor]

I can still laugh if something’s really funny… but it feels kind of muted. Most of the time it’s like the jokes have to work extra hard to reach me, and even then the laughter fades fast.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[quietly]  
Not really... I mean, I can laugh a little if my husband makes a joke, but it feels forced—like I have to remind myself to smile. Mostly nothing feels funny these days.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[shakes head slowly]

Not much... I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but now it all feels kind of flat. I still do them, hoping I’ll feel something, but the enjoyment barely shows up.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes drop to my lap, voice small]

Yeah... like when the baby wouldn't settle last night, I kept thinking it must be something I did—maybe I ate the wrong thing, or I'm not soothing him right. I know rationally babies just cry, but the guilt still sneaks in several times a day.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[nods, pulling the cardigan tighter]

Pretty often. My mind races about the baby breathing, or whether the crib’s safe, even if I just checked. There doesn’t have to be a real reason—sometimes I’m just sitting there and the worry hits out of nowhere. I can usually talk myself down, but it keeps popping back up.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[wrings hands]

A few times this week I’ve had that sudden rush—heart pounding, can’t catch my breath—like something awful is about to happen, even though the room is quiet and the baby’s fine. It passes after a minute, but it leaves me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… most days feel like I’m drowning in small stuff. I’ll be feeding the baby and notice the dishes piling up, and suddenly it’s like I can’t breathe. I manage to get through it, but it’s this constant sense of being overwhelmed, like I’m always one step behind and never going to catch up.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[exhales slowly]

A few nights this week I lay there staring at the ceiling even when the baby was asleep. My thoughts just loop—worrying I’m not doing enough, feeling sad, and then I’m more awake. I finally drift off, but it takes forever, and I wake up again with my mind racing.
I have felt sad or miserable

[soft voice, eyes glassy]

Most of the day, yeah. It’s like a heaviness I can’t shake. I still smile for the baby, but inside I feel flat or weepy. Yesterday I cried while folding laundry—no real reason, just this wave of sadness.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[nods, voice cracking]

Yeah… I’ve cried a couple of times this week. Once was after a feeding, when the baby finally settled—instead of feeling relieved I just burst into tears. Another time I saw a diaper commercial and couldn’t stop. It’s like the tears sit right under the surface lately.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[long pause, eyes fixed on the floor]

Once or twice, in the worst moments… it’s not that I want to do anything, but the thought flashes—like “what if I just weren’t here?” It scares me, and I push it away. I don’t have a plan or any real wish to hurt myself—I just want the sadness and pressure to stop.

You've shared how the last week has felt heavy-laughing feels forced, things you used to enjoy now feel flat, and worries about the baby race through your mind even when everything is objectively fine. You described sudden waves of panic, nights spent staring at the ceiling re-playing every possible failing, and tears that arrive without warning. In the hardest moments a frightening thought of not wanting to be here has flickered across your mind, though you quickly push it away.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports minimal, forced laughter and states "nothing feels funny these days," aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurring self-blame several times daily, matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intrusive worries occurring "pretty often" without triggers, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes classic panic attacks occurring multiple times this week without identifiable triggers, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm ('most days') and physical anxiety symptoms ('can't breathe'), indicating intermittent difficulty coping, matching 'sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly insomnia driven by persistent unhappiness and racing thoughts, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sadness "most of the day" with frequent crying and persistent low mood, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple crying episodes triggered by minor events, indicating frequent tearfulness consistent with "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports intrusive passive suicidal thoughts occurring "once or twice" but denies intent/plan, aligning with "Sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** With a score of 25 you meet the EPDS high-risk cutoff (≥14) indicating probable <med>postpartum depression</med>. You endorse core criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartonset</med>: depressed mood most of the day, markedly diminished interest or pleasure, feelings of worthlessness/guilt, diminished ability to think or concentrate, and recurrent thoughts of death. Significant <sym>anxiety</sym> and <sym>panic attacks</sym> suggest co-occurring <med>perinatal anxiety</med>. Item 10 ≥1 mandates immediate safety assessment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med>
2. Call the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline 1-833-943-5746 (24/7, confidential) or 988 if distress escalates
3. Enlist trusted adult to stay with you and baby until professional review
4. Ask doctor about evidence-based treatments: <med>CBT</med>, <med>IPT</med>, or <med>antidepressant medication</med> compatible with breastfeeding
5. Practice 20-30 minutes daily gentle movement or outdoor walk if medically cleared
6. Aim for 4-5 hour stretches of sleep: split night duties with support person, nap when baby naps
7. Limit information overload-mute social media, pare to-do list to feeding, hydration, and rest
8. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 1-2 weeks to track progress
9. Keep emergency plan: local ER or 911 if thoughts of self-harm intensify
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Presenting symptoms (mother’s own words paraphrased):
- Marked anhedonia: reports little to no amusement or anticipatory enjoyment; activities feel “flat”
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, crying spells (≥ 3–4× this week) unrelated to circumstance
- Excessive self-blame/guilt about infant care (“something I did”)
- Unwarranted, intrusive worries (infant safety) and episodic panic sensations (heart racing, breathlessness)
- Feeling “drowning” or overwhelmed by routine tasks; difficulty “catching up”
- Sleep-onset and maintenance disturbance linked to ruminative worry and sadness
- Passive self-harm ideation without intent or plan (“what if I just weren’t here?”)

Pattern: Symptoms present most of the day, nearly every day, over the past two weeks; interfere with daily functioning and parenting tasks.

Potential screening significance: High endorsement of core depressive symptoms plus prominent anxiety; meets EPDS clinical-cutoff range on items 1–9; item 10 ≥1 warrants safety evaluation.

Risk flags:
- Passive suicidal thoughts → immediate safety assessment indicated
- Significant impairment in mood, coping, sleep, and self-appraisal consistent with moderate–severe postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety

Plan: Discuss results, offer supportive validation, review emergency/safety resources, coordinate expedited follow-up (OB, PCP, or perinatal psychiatry) for comprehensive evaluation and possible treatment options.
